name: Colin Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not much to tell, really. I'm Colin, 27, I live with my girlfriend Jess in a small rented house in Brenford. She works behind the counter at the pharmacy on the main street. I work at Harlow Packaging, the cardboard box plant out on the industrial estate, been there about eight months.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the second man on the folder-gluer, which is a long machine that takes flat sheets of corrugated board, prints on them, folds them and glues them into boxes. I feed the sheets in at one end and stack the bundles at the other, and I clean the ink rollers at the end of the shift, which is a filthy job. Steve, the operator, does all the settings, and he's not very patient when I get the sheets in skewed. I don't mind it, it's steady, and I like that I can switch my brain off a bit and think about fishing at the reservoir on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never really paid it much attention anyway. Maybe at break I'd say, see, all that fuss over nothing. I'm not online much, I don't post things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, which is fine by me. I don't use any of that AI stuff, Jess has it on her phone but I've never touched it. My job's about feeding a machine, I can't see a computer program doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just keep doing what I'm doing. Turn up, do my shifts, maybe in a year or two Steve teaches me the settings and I get a bit more money. I'd like to get the car's clutch done, that's the next big thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal. Bit like hearing the weather's going to be the same as yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a computer couldn't feed the machine. Are there any robots at Harlow already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a palletiser at the end of Line 1, it's a robot arm that stacks the finished bundles onto pallets. Used to be two guys on that. One retired and the other went onto nights, I think, so nobody really lost out. That's how it should work, if you ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money like at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight, but we get by. I've got maybe two hundred spare at the end of most months before the car takes it. If something big went, like the boiler, I'd have to ask my dad, which I'd rather not.

S0.say: He'd say he never paid much attention and that it was fuss over nothing. He doesn't post online.
S0.think: He thinks nothing changes, which suits him, since he doesn't use AI and can't see a program feeding his machine. He sees his job as safe from software.
S0.do: Keeps working his shifts and hopes the operator teaches him the settings within a year or two for a small raise. Plans to get his car's clutch repaired next.
S0.feel: Fine and normal, like the weather staying the same.
S0.quote: My job's about feeding a machine, I can't see a computer program doing that.
S0.fieldNote: Colin keeps the topic at arm's length and has never tried an AI tool. He's comfortable with the palletiser robot because nobody visibly lost out. He measures his life in small fixed goals like the car's clutch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it's just how things go, companies always find a cheaper way. I wouldn't make a fuss about it. If people asked, I'd say I'd see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried. I'm the guy who feeds the sheets in and stacks the bundles, and that's exactly the bit they'd automate, they already did it on Line 1. And there's nothing else round here, Harlow and the frozen food place and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job as well as I can, so they keep me over someone else. I'd stop going out on Fridays and I'd put off the clutch, just drive it carefully. I wouldn't go looking for courses, I'm not a classroom person, I'd wait and see what the company does first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick, like when you get a letter from the bank and you don't want to open it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they actually announced it, I suppose. A notice on the board saying Line 2's getting a robot feeder. Until there's a notice, it's just talk, and I've heard a lot of talk in eight months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to Jess about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, not until something happens. She'd worry, and then she'd start looking up courses for me, and I'd feel pushed. I'd rather sort it in my own head first.

S1.say: He'd say companies always find cheaper ways and he wouldn't make a fuss. If asked, he'd say he'd see what happens.
S1.think: Privately he'd be worried, because feeding and stacking are exactly what's being automated, as already happened on Line 1. With almost no similar jobs nearby, losing this one would leave him stuck.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and works hard so he's kept over others. Stops Friday nights out and delays the clutch repair, and holds off on any courses until the company announces something.
S1.feel: A bit sick, like an unopened letter from the bank.
S1.quote: Until there's a notice, it's just talk, and I've heard a lot of talk in eight months.
S1.fieldNote: His public shrug hides real worry, and he avoids sharing it even with his girlfriend. He waits for a formal notice before he'll act. He doesn't blame anyone; to him it's just how companies are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably not much. Maybe that the government should've seen it coming, but they never see anything coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be out. No two ways about it. I'm the newest, I'm on the lowest pay, I'm not that good at the job yet, and if a robot can do everything, they don't need Steve either, never mind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything that isn't rent and food, and I'd sell the car if I had to, even though I'd hate it. When the job went, I'd take whatever I could get, delivery, cleaning, anything with a pay packet. If that dried up, we'd have to go back to my dad's in Kettleby, him and my stepmum, and Jess would hate that more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't think I'd know what to do for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Jess would hate moving to your dad's. What would happen with her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing, she'd keep hers longer than me, probably, people still need someone at the pharmacy to talk to. So she'd be the one paying, and I'd be sitting at home. I don't know how I'd handle that, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned delivery or cleaning. Wouldn't robots be doing that too in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I suppose. I hadn't thought it through. I just know I'd grab whatever was going, because sitting still with no money isn't an option. But if there's nothing going, there's nothing going.

S2.say: He wouldn't say much in public, maybe that the government should have seen it coming. He'd add that governments never see anything coming.
S2.think: He's sure he'd be out, as the newest, lowest-paid and least skilled, and thinks even the experienced operator wouldn't be needed.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent and food and would sell the car if needed. After losing the job, takes any paid work such as delivery or cleaning, and if that fails moves with his partner into his father's house.
S2.feel: Like the floor has gone, unsure what to do for a while.
S2.quote: She'd be the one paying, and I'd be sitting at home. I don't know how I'd handle that, honestly.
S2.fieldNote: He admits he hadn't thought through that the fallback jobs would be automated too, and that realisation left him with nothing. The idea of his partner supporting him clearly bothers him more than the job itself. His blame for government is mild and resigned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least there's some warning this time. People should get ready. I'd still keep my head down at work, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd see it coming, which almost makes it worse. I'd be 32 and still on the bottom rung at Harlow if I'm honest. I'm not someone who reinvents himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save, even if it's fifty a month, so there's something there. I'd ask Steve to teach me the settings properly, because at least then I'm worth more for longer. And I'd keep an eye on jobs at the council, waste collection or the parks, because councils are slow to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. It'd sit in the back of my head every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's been on waste collection for twenty years. Councils never have money for new stuff, they still use the same trucks from when I was at school. So I'd think they'd be last to bring in robots, if they ever do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said seeing it coming almost makes it worse. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then every day you're waiting for the notice. With the fast one it just happens, it's awful but it's done. This way I'd be lying awake for five years, like the clock's ticking on the wall.

S3.say: He'd say at least there's warning this time and people should prepare, while he keeps his head down at work.
S3.think: He thinks seeing it coming almost makes it worse and expects to still be on the bottom rung at 32. He doesn't see himself reinventing himself.
S3.do: Tries to save about fifty a month and asks the operator to teach him the settings properly to stay useful longer. Watches for council jobs such as waste collection or parks, which he thinks will be slow to automate.
S3.feel: Worried, a constant thought in the back of every shift.
S3.quote: With the fast one it just happens, it's awful but it's done. This way I'd be lying awake for five years, like the clock's ticking on the wall.
S3.fieldNote: An unusual reaction: for him the warning period itself is a source of dread. His plan is cautious, looking for the slowest-moving employer he knows. His logic about councils comes from his uncle's experience, not research.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'd say that's ages, loads can change in ten years. Probably wouldn't think about it much day to day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37, and maybe I'd have moved to the council by then, or got good at the folder-gluer. I'd probably be alright for most of that time. It's the end bit I can't picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Harlow and try to get the settings learned. I'd put something aside each month, more once the car's sorted. If a council job came up in the next few years I'd go for it, and otherwise I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could push it to the back of my mind. Ten years is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change anything about your plans with Jess, like moving in somewhere permanent or getting married?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about getting married, maybe in a couple of years. I don't think this would stop that. If anything you'd want someone with you, wouldn't you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push it to the back of your mind. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, honestly. I know Jess would say I'm burying my head. But I can't spend ten years worrying, I'd be no use to anyone.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is ages and a lot can change, and that he wouldn't think about it much day to day.
S4.think: He thinks he'd probably be fine for most of the decade, maybe at the council or skilled on the folder-gluer by 37. It's the end he can't picture.
S4.do: Carries on at the box plant learning the settings and puts money aside monthly, more once the car is fixed. Applies for council jobs if they come up and otherwise waits to see.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to push it to the back of his mind.
S4.quote: I can't spend ten years worrying, I'd be no use to anyone.
S4.fieldNote: A decade lets his usual coping style, not thinking about it, work again. He admits it's part plan, part hope. His wedding plans hold firm and he even says the threat makes partnership feel more important.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There'd be nothing to grab hold of. What would help, I suppose, is just a job, any job, that a person still has to do, and enough money in between so we don't lose the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about places like Brenford. It's all fine talking about new jobs appearing, but they never appear here. They appear in the city, and I can't afford to live in the city.

headlineQuote: It's all fine talking about new jobs appearing, but they never appear here. They appear in the city, and I can't afford to live in the city.
portrait: Colin Schmidt is a 27-year-old second man on a folder-gluer at a cardboard box plant in a small town with almost no other factory jobs. He's never used an AI tool, prefers to switch his brain off at work, and copes with worry by not talking about it, even with his girlfriend Jess. He's calm in the plateau, quietly anxious in steady change and floored by AGI in two years, when he realises even the fallback jobs he'd grab would be gone. Oddly, five years of warning feels almost worse to him than a sudden shock. He blames no one much and looks for the slowest-changing employer he knows, the council.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be nothing to grab hold of.
whatWouldHelp: A job of any kind that a person still has to do, and enough money in between so they don't lose their home.
